abstract: |
  Christopher Nolan's *Oppenheimer* (2023) moves through about thirty years
  of physics: molecular quantum mechanics in 1927, neutron stars and
  gravitational collapse in 1939, fission, the bomb, and the hydrogen bomb
  debate. This review collects what historians and physicists have written
  about the film, then takes each piece of physics in the order the film
  meets it. For each one it gives the paper or report where the work first
  appeared, the key equations, and a short calculation that checks the
  numbers.
jupyter: python3

::: {.callout-note}
Written by Claude as a reading guide. Every journal article in the
bibliography was checked against Crossref, and every textbook section
number against the book. Scene descriptions come from
memory of the film and from the reviews cited, so check any claim about what
is on screen against the film itself. Calculations use textbook models and
stated inputs; they reproduce orders of magnitude and some classic results,
not design figures.
:::


# How to read the film's physics

The film covers three periods, and each one leaves a different paper trail.

**1926 to 1939: open literature.** Everything Oppenheimer and his
contemporaries did before the war appeared in ordinary journals:
*Zeitschrift für Physik*, *Annalen der Physik*, *Physical Review*,
*Nature*. These are the papers to read alongside the early scenes. The
issue of *Physical Review* dated 1 September 1939, the day Germany invaded
Poland, holds both Bohr and Wheeler's theory of fission
[@bohr1939wheeler] and Oppenheimer and Snyder's paper on collapse
[@oppenheimer1939snyder].

**1940 to 1945: secrecy.** Physicists in Britain and the United States
began holding back fission results in 1940, before any government required
it. The system leaked at first. McMillan and Abelson published the
discovery of neptunium in June 1940 [@mcmillan1940], and Flerov and Petrzhak
published spontaneous fission in *Physical Review* that summer
[@flerov1940]. By 1941 the controls held: Seaborg, McMillan, Kennedy and
Wahl's letter on element 94 reached *Physical Review* on 28 January 1941
and waited until 1946 [@seaborg1946]. Wartime work went into numbered
Los Alamos reports instead: LA-1 (Serber's lectures, published as
@serber1992) and LA-602 on atmospheric ignition [@konopinski1946].
@wellerstein2021 tells the story of this system.

**1945 onward: release in stages.** The Smyth Report [@smyth1945] was the
first official account. The withheld papers followed in 1946
[@seaborg1946; @kennedy1946], and the Los Alamos reports came out over
decades. Some details of weapon design remain classified. Academics also
worked results out from the outside: G. I. Taylor estimated the Trinity
yield in 1950 from published photographs [@taylor1950a; @taylor1950b],
which @sec-trinity repeats.

So "the original paper" means a journal article for the scenes up to 1939,
an internal report for the Los Alamos scenes, and often a post-war
reconstruction for the bomb physics itself. @reed2021 rebuilds that physics
from open sources and is the best single companion to the middle of the
film. @hoddeson1993 is the technical history of Los Alamos.

# What reviewers said {#sec-reviews}

No full-length scholarly study of the film's physics has appeared. The
closest pieces are reviews and letters.

**Historians.** @whitfield2024 reviews the film for the *Journal of
American History*. He reads it as narrowing a large scientific and
political effort down to one man. @griffith2023 goes scene by scene for the
*Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists* and finds the technical content mostly
faithful. He calls the marbles-in-bowls scene invented, though it conveys
the scale of the isotope problem. He notes that Rutherford, not Blackett,
introduced Oppenheimer to Bohr, and that the film gives the
atmospheric-ignition question more weight than it had in 1945.
@politifact2023 found that the two Einstein scenes about ignition did not
happen; Oppenheimer took the question to Arthur Compton.

**Physicists.** A *Physics Today* exchange set the terms of the debate.
@santiago2024 argue that the film celebrates Trinity as a scientific feat
and ignores fallout and the people living downwind. @reed2024 answers that
the film is a life of Oppenheimer, not a documentary, and that it may draw
young viewers to the history. Reed is the author of @reed2021. The writers
at *Physics World* [@physicsworld2023] rated the film highly; Kate Gardner
also raised the people living near the test site. Scientists at ANSTO
wanted more physics on screen [@ansto2023]. Kevin Pitts checked the delay
between the Trinity flash and the sound and found it right
[@pitts2023]. In an interview with *Science*, the historian David Cassidy
called Oppenheimer "no Einstein" but rated the collapse work at Nobel level
[@cho2023]. Los Alamos published its own summary of his science
[@lanl2023].

**On the physics itself.** @ortega2017 is the best paper on why the
collapse work of 1939 went unused for two decades. It sits between history
and physics and does not depend on the film.

# Göttingen, 1927: separating electrons from nuclei

The film shows Oppenheimer arriving in Göttingen to work with Max Born. Two
papers came out of that year: his thesis on the continuous spectrum
[@oppenheimer1927] and the paper with Born that every chemistry course
still uses [@born1927].

A molecule has electrons at positions $\mathbf r$ and nuclei at positions
$\mathbf R$, with Hamiltonian
$$
H = T_N + T_e + V(\mathbf r, \mathbf R), \qquad
T_N = -\sum_a \frac{\hbar^2}{2M_a}\nabla_a^2 .
$$
Nuclei are thousands of times heavier than electrons and move slowly, so
Born and Oppenheimer first solve for the electrons with the nuclei held
still:
$$
\bigl[T_e + V(\mathbf r; \mathbf R)\bigr]\,\phi_k(\mathbf r; \mathbf R)
  = U_k(\mathbf R)\,\phi_k(\mathbf r; \mathbf R).
$$
The electronic energy $U_k(\mathbf R)$ then acts as the potential for the
nuclei:
$$
\bigl[T_N + U_k(\mathbf R)\bigr]\,\chi(\mathbf R) = E\,\chi(\mathbf R),
\qquad
\Psi(\mathbf r, \mathbf R) \approx \phi_k(\mathbf r; \mathbf R)\,\chi(\mathbf R).
$$
Born and Oppenheimer expanded in the small parameter
$\kappa = (m_e/M)^{1/4}$ and found the familiar ordering of molecular
energies:
$$
E_{\text{electronic}} : E_{\text{vibration}} : E_{\text{rotation}}
  \approx 1 : \kappa^2 : \kappa^4 .
$$

::: {#53e35b33 .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
kappa = (m_e / m_p) ** 0.25
print(f"H2: kappa = {kappa:.3f}, kappa^2 = {kappa**2:.4f}, "
      f"kappa^4 = {kappa**4:.5f}")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
H2: kappa = 0.153, kappa^2 = 0.0233, kappa^4 = 0.00054
```
:::
:::


For hydrogen, with $M = m_p$, that gives $\kappa \approx$
0\.15: vibrational energies a few per cent of
electronic ones, rotational energies a few parts in ten thousand. That
matches spectra (electronic transitions in the ultraviolet, vibrations in
the infrared, rotations in the microwave).

*Textbooks:* @landau1977qm [§78], @tong2017topics [§2.3.6], and @shankar1994 [§21.1, under "The Berry Phase"], which derives the separation from the path integral.

# Heisenberg's lecture: uncertainty

The film puts Oppenheimer, with Rabi, in the audience for a Heisenberg
lecture. The paper of that year is @heisenberg1927, which argued from
thought experiments that position and momentum cannot both be exact,
roughly $\delta x\,\delta p \sim h$. The inequality in its modern form,
$$
\sigma_x \sigma_p \ge \frac{\hbar}{2},
$$
with $\sigma$ the standard deviation, came from @kennard1927 soon after.

*Textbooks:* @landau1977qm [§16], @tongqm [§3.4.1] and @shankar1994 [ch. 9].

# Berkeley in the 1930s

The film compresses Oppenheimer's Berkeley years into a few scenes of
teaching and of Lawrence's Radiation Laboratory. The physics behind them is
mostly not on screen, but it explains his reputation.

## Tunnelling

@oppenheimer1928 includes one of the first uses of quantum tunnelling: an
electric field $F$ can pull the electron out of a hydrogen atom even though
classically it is bound. In the WKB approximation the probability of
crossing a barrier is
$$
T \approx \exp\!\left(-\frac{2}{\hbar}\int \sqrt{2m\,[V(x) - E]}\,\mathrm dx\right),
$$
and for an electron bound by energy $W$ in a uniform field, the barrier
$V - E = W - eFx$ is a triangle, giving
$$
T \approx \exp\!\left(-\frac{4\sqrt{2m}\,W^{3/2}}{3\hbar e F}\right).
$$
The same exponent governs field emission from metals (Fowler and Nordheim,
also 1928).

*Textbooks:* barrier penetration is in @landau1977qm [§50], and the ionisation of hydrogen by an electric field, the problem Oppenheimer tackled, is worked in @landau1977qm [§77, Problem 1]. @tong2017topics [§§2.2.5, 4.1] and @shankar1994 [§16.2] cover the same ground.

## The anti-electron

Dirac's equation allows negative energies, $E = \pm\sqrt{p^2c^2 + m^2c^4}$.
Dirac first suggested that the "holes" in the filled sea of negative-energy
states were protons. @oppenheimer1930 pointed out that the electron in a
hydrogen atom would then fall into its proton's hole, so hydrogen would
annihilate within a tiny fraction of a second. Weyl showed in the same
period that the theory's symmetry forces the hole to have the electron's
mass. @dirac1931 accepted both points and predicted the anti-electron,
which @anderson1933 found in cosmic rays.

*Textbooks:* @tong2006qft [§5.3], @tongpp [§2.1.3] and @shankar1994 [§20.3]. @tongpp explains why the Dirac sea, though it led to the right prediction, is the wrong picture.

## Deuterons and the Coulomb barrier

A charged particle hitting a nucleus must climb the Coulomb barrier,
$$
V_C = \frac{Z_1 Z_2 e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0\,R}, \qquad
R \approx r_0\bigl(A_1^{1/3} + A_2^{1/3}\bigr),\quad r_0 \approx 1.2~\text{fm}.
$$
@oppenheimer1935 explained why deuterons react with heavy nuclei at
energies below this barrier. The deuteron is large and loosely bound
(2.2 MeV). The nucleus repels its proton, which leaves the neutron in front
to be captured while the proton flies off. This (d, p) reaction is the
Oppenheimer–Phillips process.

*Textbooks:* @landau1977qm [§50, Problem 2] derive the tunnelling factor through a Coulomb barrier, first found by Gamow. @krane1988 [§8.4] uses it for alpha decay, and covers the deuteron in §4.1 and stripping reactions in §11.11.

## Lawrence's cyclotron

A charge $q$ in a field $B$ circles at the cyclotron frequency, which does
not depend on its speed:
$$
\omega_c = \frac{qB}{m}, \qquad K_{\max} = \frac{q^2 B^2 R^2}{2m},
$$
so a fixed-frequency oscillator can kick it twice per turn as it spirals
out to the magnet's radius $R$ [@lawrence1932]. The same magnets later
became the calutrons of @sec-materials.

*Textbooks:* @landau1975fields [§21], @tong2013dynrel [§2.4.2] and @krane1988 [§15.2].

# Stars, 1938–1939: neutron cores and collapse {#sec-stars}

The film gives one scene to this work: Oppenheimer and Hartland Snyder
talking through what happens when a star exhausts its fuel. It is the work
modern physicists rate highest [@cho2023; @ortega2017].

## The sequence of papers

@landau1938 proposed that stars might have neutron cores.
@oppenheimer1938 showed that such cores are unstable unless they are large.
@tolman1939 and @oppenheimer1939volkoff, back to back in *Physical Review*,
set up the general-relativistic equations of stellar structure and found a
maximum mass for a star held up by neutron degeneracy pressure.
@oppenheimer1939snyder then asked what happens above it.

## The Tolman–Oppenheimer–Volkoff equation

For a static, spherically symmetric star with pressure $P(r)$, mass-energy
density $\varepsilon(r)$ and enclosed mass $m(r)$, general relativity
replaces Newtonian hydrostatic equilibrium with
$$
\frac{\mathrm dP}{\mathrm dr} =
 -\frac{G\,\bigl(\varepsilon/c^2 + P/c^2\bigr)\bigl(m + 4\pi r^3 P/c^2\bigr)}
       {r^2\bigl(1 - 2Gm/rc^2\bigr)},
\qquad
\frac{\mathrm dm}{\mathrm dr} = \frac{4\pi r^2 \varepsilon}{c^2}.
$$
Each of the three corrections to Newton makes gravity stronger: pressure
gravitates, it adds to the enclosed mass, and the metric factor diverges
as $r \to 2Gm/c^2$. Oppenheimer and Volkoff closed the system with the
equation of state of a cold ideal Fermi gas of neutrons. With
$x = p_F/m_n c$,
$$
\varepsilon = \frac{m_n^4 c^5}{8\pi^2\hbar^3}
  \Bigl[x(2x^2+1)\sqrt{1+x^2} - \sinh^{-1}x\Bigr],\qquad
P = \frac{m_n^4 c^5}{24\pi^2\hbar^3}
  \Bigl[x(2x^2-3)\sqrt{1+x^2} + 3\sinh^{-1}x\Bigr].
$$

::: {#cell-fig-tov .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp

K = m_n**4 * c**5 / (np.pi**2 * hbar**3)

# The exact forms cancel badly for small x, so below x = 0.01 use their
# leading terms: rest mass for eps, the non-relativistic gas for P.
def eps_of_x(x):
    exact = x * (2 * x**2 + 1) * np.sqrt(1 + x**2) - np.arcsinh(x)
    return K / 8 * np.where(x < 0.01, 8 / 3 * x**3, exact)

def P_of_x(x):
    exact = x * (2 * x**2 - 3) * np.sqrt(1 + x**2) + 3 * np.arcsinh(x)
    return K / 24 * np.where(x < 0.01, 8 / 5 * x**5, exact)

# Tabulate the equation of state once and interpolate eps(P) in log P.
x_tab = np.logspace(-4, 2, 4000)
logP_tab, eps_tab = np.log(P_of_x(x_tab)), eps_of_x(x_tab)

def tov(r, y):
    P, m = y
    if P <= 0:
        return [0.0, 0.0]
    eps = np.interp(np.log(P), logP_tab, eps_tab)
    dP = (-G * (eps + P) / c**2 * (m + 4 * np.pi * r**3 * P / c**2)
          / (r**2 * (1 - 2 * G * m / (r * c**2))))
    return [dP, 4 * np.pi * r**2 * eps / c**2]

def star(x_c):
    """Radius (m) and gravitational mass (kg) for central Fermi momentum x_c."""
    P_c, r0 = P_of_x(x_c), 1.0
    surface = lambda r, y: y[0] - 1e-10 * P_c
    surface.terminal = True
    sol = solve_ivp(tov, [r0, 1e6], [P_c, 4 / 3 * np.pi * r0**3
                                      * eps_of_x(x_c) / c**2],
                    events=surface, rtol=1e-8, max_step=200,
                    atol=[1e-14 * P_c, 1e10])
    return sol.t[-1], sol.y[1, -1]

x_c = np.logspace(-0.7, 1.3, 60)
R_star, M_star = np.array([star(x) for x in x_c]).T
i_max = np.argmax(M_star)
M_OV, R_OV = M_star[i_max] / M_sun, R_star[i_max] / 1e3

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3.2))
ax.plot(R_star / 1e3, M_star / M_sun)
ax.plot(R_OV, M_OV, "o")
ax.annotate(f"{M_OV:.2f} $M_\\odot$ at {R_OV:.1f} km", (R_OV, M_OV),
            xytext=(12, -4), textcoords="offset points")
ax.set_xlabel("radius (km)")
ax.set_ylabel(r"mass ($M_\odot$)")
ax.set_xlim(0, 40)
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Mass against radius for stars of free neutrons, from integrating the TOV equation outward from the centre for a range of central densities. The maximum is the Oppenheimer–Volkoff limit.](index_files/figure-html/fig-tov-output-1.png){#fig-tov width=450 height=297}
:::
:::


The maximum in @fig-tov is a gravitational mass of
0\.71 $M_\odot$ at a radius of
9\.3 km. @landau1980stat [§109] quote
$0.76\,M_\odot$ at 9.4 km for the same model. Their figure is the rest mass
$N m_n$ of the neutrons, which exceeds the gravitational mass by the
binding energy. Observed neutron stars reach about two solar masses,
because nuclear forces stiffen the equation of state well beyond a free
Fermi gas. The qualitative result stands: above some mass, no cold star can
support itself.

*Textbooks:* @landau1975fields [§100] set up the field equations inside matter, from which the TOV equation follows; @landau1980stat [§§106–109] cover dense matter and the neutron-star limit; @carroll2004 [§5.8] derives the TOV equation. For the Newtonian version of the degeneracy argument, see the white dwarfs and the Chandrasekhar limit in @tongstat [§3.6.5].

## Oppenheimer–Snyder collapse

@oppenheimer1939snyder took the simplest case, a uniform ball of
pressureless dust starting from rest, and solved Einstein's equations
exactly. Outside the ball the metric is Schwarzschild's, with gravitational
radius $r_g = 2GM/c^2$. Two results matter.

For an observer riding on the surface, the collapse takes a finite proper
time, the same as Newtonian free fall from rest at radius $R_0$:
$$
\tau = \frac{\pi}{2}\sqrt{\frac{R_0^3}{2GM}}.
$$

::: {#0f6f66e9 .cell execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
R_sun = 6.957e8
tau_sun = np.pi / 2 * np.sqrt(R_sun**3 / (2 * G * M_sun))
r_g_sun = 2 * G * M_sun / c**2
print(f"tau = {tau_sun:.0f} s, r_g = {r_g_sun/1e3:.2f} km")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
tau = 1769 s, r_g = 2.95 km
```
:::
:::


A ball with the Sun's mass and radius would collapse in about
29 minutes of its own time, through a
gravitational radius of 3\.0 km.

For a distant observer, the surface never quite reaches $r_g$. A radially
falling surface obeys, in Schwarzschild time $t$,
$\mathrm dr/\mathrm dt \to -c\,(1 - r_g/r)$ as $r \to r_g$, so
$$
r - r_g \propto \exp(-ct/r_g).
$$
The approach takes a time of order $r_g/c$, tens of microseconds for a
solar mass, after which light from the surface is redshifted beyond
detection. Oppenheimer and Snyder put it as the star tending "to close
itself off from any communication with a distant observer". Landau and
Lifshitz work through the same solution in modern coordinates
[@landau1975fields, §§102–103].

*Textbooks:* besides @landau1975fields [§§102–103], @tong2019gr [§§6.1.2–6.1.5] covers the horizon, the coordinates that cross it, and the formation of black holes by collapse, and @carroll2004 [§§5.6–5.8] does the same.

## Why nobody followed it up

The paper describes what Wheeler named a black hole in 1967. The
@ortega2017 paper asks why it sat unused for two decades. One reason is
on screen in the film's Einstein scenes, though the film does not make the
link: in October 1939 @einstein1939 published a model of a cluster of
particles in circular orbits and concluded that Schwarzschild
singularities "do not exist in physical reality". Oppenheimer himself never
returned to the subject. Freeman Dyson called the collapse paper his one
revolutionary contribution to science [@cho2023].

# January 1939: fission {#sec-fission}

The film shows Luis Alvarez reading about fission in a barber's chair,
rushing to tell Oppenheimer, and the oscilloscope that showed the
ionisation pulses of fission fragments. Oppenheimer first says it can't
happen, then works out on the blackboard that it releases neutrons, and
those neutrons could make a bomb.

## The discovery

@hahn1939 found barium among the products of uranium bombarded with
neutrons. @meitner1939 explained it with Bohr's liquid-drop model: the
nucleus stretches and splits, and the two charged fragments fly apart.
@frisch1939 then saw the fragments' ionisation pulses directly, the
experiment Alvarez repeated at Berkeley.

## How much energy

Meitner and Frisch estimated the energy two ways. The mass of a uranium
nucleus exceeds that of the two fragments by about a fifth of a proton
mass, about 200 MeV. Alternatively, two fragments of charge $Ze/2$
touching each other carry Coulomb energy
$$
E \approx \frac{(Z/2)^2 e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 \cdot 2R_f},\qquad
R_f = r_0 (A/2)^{1/3}.
$$

::: {#6128e14b .cell execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code}
Z, A, r0 = 92, 236, 1.2e-15
R_f = r0 * (A / 2) ** (1 / 3)
E_touch = k_C * (Z / 2) ** 2 * e**2 / (2 * R_f) / MeV
print(f"two touching fragments: {E_touch:.0f} MeV")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
two touching fragments: 259 MeV
```
:::
:::


This gives 259 MeV, an overestimate because real
fragments are deformed and unequal, but the right size. A chemical
reaction releases a few eV per molecule, so fission is about $10^8$ times
more energetic per event.

## The liquid-drop barrier

@bohr1939wheeler made the model quantitative. In the semi-empirical mass
formula the surface energy is $E_S = a_s A^{2/3}$ and the Coulomb energy
is $E_C = a_c Z^2/A^{1/3}$. Stretch the sphere into a slight spheroid with
deformation $\alpha_2$; to second order
$$
E_S(\alpha_2) = E_S\Bigl(1 + \tfrac{2}{5}\alpha_2^2\Bigr),\qquad
E_C(\alpha_2) = E_C\Bigl(1 - \tfrac{1}{5}\alpha_2^2\Bigr).
$$
The surface resists deformation and the charge favours it. The sphere
becomes unstable when $E_C > 2E_S$, which defines the fissility
$$
x = \frac{E_C}{2E_S} = \frac{a_c}{2a_s}\,\frac{Z^2}{A}.
$$

::: {#7d2b1cd0 .cell execution_count=6}
``` {.python .cell-code}
a_s, a_c = 17.8, 0.711   # MeV, one standard fit of the mass formula
Z2A_crit = 2 * a_s / a_c
x_U235 = 92**2 / 235 / Z2A_crit
print(f"(Z^2/A)_crit = {Z2A_crit:.1f}, U-235: Z^2/A = {92**2/235:.1f}, "
      f"x = {x_U235:.2f}")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
(Z^2/A)_crit = 50.1, U-235: Z^2/A = 36.0, x = 0.72
```
:::
:::


The critical value of $Z^2/A$ is about 50.
Uranium has $Z^2/A \approx 36$ and $x \approx$ 0\.72,
so it sits behind a barrier of a few MeV. A neutron has to bring in enough
energy to get over it.

## Why only uranium-235

@bohr1939resonance argued that slow neutrons split the rare isotope
uranium-235, not the common uranium-238. The reason is pairing: nuclei with
even numbers of neutrons are more tightly bound. A neutron joining
uranium-235 makes even–even uranium-236 and releases its full binding
energy. A neutron joining uranium-238 makes odd uranium-239 and releases
less. The neutron separation energy is
$S_n(A{+}1) = [M(A) + m_n - M(A{+}1)]\,c^2$.

::: {#a192990a .cell execution_count=7}
``` {.python .cell-code}
S_n_236 = (mass["U235"] + mass["n"] - mass["U236"]) * u_MeV
S_n_239 = (mass["U238"] + mass["n"] - mass["U239"]) * u_MeV
print(f"S_n(U-236) = {S_n_236:.2f} MeV, S_n(U-239) = {S_n_239:.2f} MeV")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
S_n(U-236) = 6.55 MeV, S_n(U-239) = 4.81 MeV
```
:::
:::


Capture by uranium-235 brings 6\.5 MeV, above the
fission barrier of about 6 MeV, so even a neutron at rest causes fission.
Capture by uranium-238 brings only 4\.8 MeV, so the
neutron itself needs about a MeV of kinetic energy. Uranium-238 is 99.3%
of natural uranium, and this is why the film's Bohr tells Oppenheimer the
whole country would have to become a factory.

*Textbooks:* @krane1988 covers binding energies and the semi-empirical mass formula (§3.3), the liquid-drop barrier (§13.1) and the energy released (§13.3).

## Secondary neutrons

The blackboard step in the film, from fission to a bomb, needs fission to
release more neutrons than it absorbs. Three groups measured this within
weeks in spring 1939 [@halban1939; @anderson1939; @szilard1939] and found
two to three per fission.

*Textbooks:* @krane1988 [§13.2], which also covers delayed neutrons.

# Chain reactions and critical mass {#sec-critical}

## Growth

If each fission produces $\nu$ neutrons and each neutron causes another
fission after a generation time $\tau$, the number of neutrons grows as
$$
N(t) = N_0 \exp\!\left(\frac{(\nu - 1)\,t}{\tau}\right) \quad\text{or, per
generation,}\quad N_g = N_0\,\nu^{g}.
$$
For fast neutrons, $\tau$ is the mean free path for fission divided by the
neutron speed.

::: {#961c53eb .cell execution_count=8}
``` {.python .cell-code}
rho_U = 18.71                          # g/cm^3, U-235 metal
n_U = rho_U / 235.04 * N_A             # nuclei per cm^3
sigma_f, sigma_el, nu = 1.235e-24, 4.566e-24, 2.637  # cm^2, 2 MeV neutrons
lam_f = 1 / (n_U * sigma_f)            # cm
lam_t = 1 / (n_U * (sigma_f + sigma_el))
v_n = np.sqrt(2 * 2 * MeV / m_n)       # m/s, 2 MeV neutron
tau_gen = lam_f / 100 / v_n            # s

nuclei_per_kg = 1000 / 235.04 * N_A
E_per_kg = nuclei_per_kg * 200 * MeV
gens = np.log(nuclei_per_kg) / np.log(nu)
print(f"lambda_f = {lam_f:.1f} cm, tau = {tau_gen*1e9:.1f} ns")
print(f"1 kg U-235: {E_per_kg:.2e} J = {E_per_kg/kt:.0f} kt; "
      f"{gens:.0f} generations = {gens*tau_gen*1e6:.2f} us")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
lambda_f = 16.9 cm, tau = 8.6 ns
1 kg U-235: 8.21e+13 J = 20 kt; 58 generations = 0.50 us
```
:::
:::


With the cross-sections @reed2021 uses for 2 MeV neutrons, a neutron
travels about 17 cm between fissions, which takes
9 ns. Fissioning one kilogram of uranium-235
releases 82 TJ, about
20 kilotons of TNT, and takes about
58 generations from one neutron: half a microsecond.
The bomb has to hold together for that long. Little Boy fissioned only
about one kilogram of its 64 kg of uranium.

## Critical size

Neutrons also leak out of the surface. In a sphere, production goes as the
volume and leakage as the surface, so there is a critical radius. Treat
the neutrons as diffusing with $D = \lambda_t v/3$:
$$
\frac{\partial n}{\partial t} = D\nabla^2 n + \frac{\nu - 1}{\tau}\,n .
$$
Separating variables, $n = \mathrm e^{\alpha t}\sin(kr)/r$ with
$\alpha = (\nu-1)/\tau - Dk^2$. The sphere is critical when $\alpha = 0$.
If the density vanishes at the surface, $kR = \pi$ and
$$
R_c = \pi\sqrt{\frac{\lambda_t\lambda_f}{3(\nu - 1)}}.
$$
A better boundary condition lets neutrons escape freely, so the density
falls to zero a distance beyond the surface. @reed2021 uses
$n + \tfrac{2}{3}\lambda_t\,\mathrm dn/\mathrm dr = 0$ at $r = R$.

::: {#c5d41f56 .cell execution_count=9}
``` {.python .cell-code}
from scipy.optimize import brentq

k_c = np.sqrt(3 * (nu - 1) / (lam_t * lam_f))
R_naive = np.pi / k_c
bc = lambda R: (np.sin(k_c * R) / R + 2 / 3 * lam_t
                * (k_c * np.cos(k_c * R) / R - np.sin(k_c * R) / R**2))
R_crit = brentq(bc, 1, R_naive - 1e-9)
mass_kg = lambda R: 4 / 3 * np.pi * R**3 * rho_U / 1000
print(f"n = 0 at surface: R = {R_naive:.2f} cm, M = {mass_kg(R_naive):.0f} kg")
print(f"escape condition: R = {R_crit:.2f} cm, M = {mass_kg(R_crit):.1f} kg")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
n = 0 at surface: R = 11.05 cm, M = 106 kg
escape condition: R = 8.37 cm, M = 45.9 kg
```
:::
:::


The crude boundary gives 11\.0 cm and
106 kg. The escape condition gives
8\.37 cm and 46 kg,
Reed's result, close to the measured bare critical mass of highly enriched
uranium. @zorich2015 [§5.6.3] builds a one-equation version of the same
balance between production and leakage as an exercise in differential
equations, and quotes 8.5 cm and about 50 kg.

## Kilograms, not tons

Before 1940 most physicists assumed a bomb would need tons of uranium,
because they thought of slow-neutron chains in natural uranium. The
@frisch1940 memorandum asked about fast neutrons in pure uranium-235 and
got an answer of the order of a kilogram. Their cross-section was too
large and the answer far too small, but it moved the problem from
impossible to industrial, and it started the British and then the American
projects. @serber1992 is the version the new arrivals at Los Alamos heard
in April 1943. It adds the tamper, a heavy shell that reflects neutrons
back and holds the core together a little longer, and the efficiency
problem: the core blows itself apart after a few generations at most.

*Textbooks:* @krane1988 [§13.9] on fission explosives, alongside @reed2021.

# Making the material: the marbles {#sec-materials}

The scene where Oppenheimer drops marbles into bowls, one for each month's
output of fissile material, is invented [@griffith2023], but the arithmetic
behind it is real. Natural uranium is 0.72% uranium-235. A bomb needs
something like 80 to 90%.

## Gaseous diffusion

Uranium hexafluoride molecules with the two isotopes have masses 349 and
352. At the same temperature, lighter molecules move faster and pass
through a porous barrier slightly more often. Graham's law gives the ideal
separation factor per barrier:
$$
\alpha = \sqrt{\frac{352}{349}}.
$$

::: {#2b0fe210 .cell execution_count=10}
``` {.python .cell-code}
alpha = np.sqrt(352 / 349)
x_f, x_p = 0.0072, 0.90
ratio = np.log((x_p / (1 - x_p)) / (x_f / (1 - x_f)))
stages = ratio / np.log(np.sqrt(alpha))
print(f"alpha = {alpha:.5f}; stages at sqrt(alpha) each: {stages:.0f}")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
alpha = 1.00429; stages at sqrt(alpha) each: 3329
```
:::
:::


That is $\alpha =$ 1\.0043, a change of 0.4% per pass. In
an ideal cascade each stage raises the abundance ratio $x/(1-x)$ by about
$\sqrt\alpha$, so going from 0.72% to 90% takes about
3\,300 stages. That is why the K-25 plant at Oak Ridge
was one of the largest buildings in the world.

## Calutrons

Lawrence's alternative was a mass spectrometer on an industrial scale. An
ion of charge $q$ accelerated through voltage $V$ moves on a circle of
radius
$$
r = \frac{1}{B}\sqrt{\frac{2mV}{q}}, \qquad
\frac{\Delta r}{r} = \frac{\Delta m}{2m} = \frac{3}{2 \times 238} \approx 0.6\%.
$$
After half a turn the two beams land $2\,\Delta r$ apart: about 1.5 cm for
a radius of about 1.2 m. Space charge and beam spread made it far harder
than this suggests.

## Plutonium

The other route makes a new fissile element in a reactor:
$$
{}^{238}\mathrm U + n \to {}^{239}\mathrm U
\xrightarrow{\beta^-,\ 23.5\ \text{min}} {}^{239}\mathrm{Np}
\xrightarrow{\beta^-,\ 2.36\ \text{d}} {}^{239}\mathrm{Pu}.
$$
@mcmillan1940 published the first step in open literature. The discovery
of plutonium [@seaborg1946] and its fissility [@kennedy1946] were held back
until 1946.

## Fermi's pile

Chicago Pile-1 went critical on 2 December 1942; the film mentions it only
in passing. A reactor can be controlled at all because about 0.65% of the
neutrons from uranium-235 fission come out seconds later, from decaying
fission fragments. With a small excess reactivity $k - 1$, the power grows
with period
$$
T \approx \frac{\ell_{\text{eff}}}{k - 1},
$$
where $\ell_{\text{eff}}$ is the mean neutron lifetime including the delayed
ones, about a tenth of a second. Prompt neutrons alone, with lifetimes of a
millisecond in graphite, would give periods too short for any control rod.

*Textbooks:* @krane1988 [§§13.5–13.6], which builds the multiplication factor of a pile like Fermi's from the four-factor formula.

# Igniting the atmosphere {#sec-ignition}

The film's tensest physics is Teller's worry that the bomb's heat could
start a self-sustaining fusion reaction in the air, and Oppenheimer's
"near zero". The analysis that settled it is @konopinski1946, written up
in 1946 from wartime work. The reaction they feared most was
$$
{}^{14}\mathrm N + {}^{14}\mathrm N \to {}^{24}\mathrm{Mg} + {}^4\mathrm{He}.
$$

::: {#7c8047b6 .cell execution_count=11}
``` {.python .cell-code}
Q_NN = (2 * mass["N14"] - mass["Mg24"] - mass["He4"]) * u_MeV
R_NN = 1.2e-15 * 2 * 14 ** (1 / 3)
V_NN = k_C * 7 * 7 * e**2 / R_NN / MeV
print(f"Q = {Q_NN:.1f} MeV, Coulomb barrier = {V_NN:.0f} MeV")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
Q = 17.2 MeV, Coulomb barrier = 12 MeV
```
:::
:::


The reaction releases 17\.2 MeV, but two nitrogen nuclei
must climb a Coulomb barrier of about 12 MeV, so the
rate at any plausible temperature depends on tunnelling deep under it. The
argument in LA-602 compares rates. At temperature $T$ the reaction heats
the air at a rate set by the tunnelling probability, and the air cools by
radiation and by Compton scattering of its electrons on the radiation. A
reaction spreads only if
$$
\frac{\mathrm d E_{\text{fusion}}}{\mathrm dt} >
\frac{\mathrm d E_{\text{radiation}}}{\mathrm dt}
$$
everywhere along the front. They found the losses ahead at every
temperature, by a margin that survived pessimistic choices of every
cross-section.

The history is thinner than the film suggests. Teller raised the idea at
Oppenheimer's Berkeley summer study in 1942 and Bethe dismissed it within
days [@rhodes1986; @griffith2023]. Oppenheimer discussed it with Compton,
not Einstein [@politifact2023].

*Textbooks:* the Coulomb-barrier tunnelling factor is in @landau1977qm [§50, Problem 2], and @krane1988 [§§14.1–14.2] applies it to fusion rates.

# Plutonium and implosion

## Why the gun fails for plutonium

Reactor plutonium contains some plutonium-240, which fissions
spontaneously and emits neutrons. A gun brings two subcritical pieces
together at a few hundred metres per second, so assembly takes a fraction
of a millisecond. A stray neutron in that window starts the chain early,
in a barely critical configuration, and the bomb fizzles.

::: {#0186b183 .cell execution_count=12}
``` {.python .cell-code}
core_g, f_240, sf_rate = 6200, 0.01, 1000   # g, mass fraction, n/(g s)
t_assemble = 0.1 / 300                      # s: 10 cm at 300 m/s
n_source = core_g * f_240 * sf_rate
print(f"{n_source:.0f} neutrons/s, {n_source * t_assemble:.0f} "
      f"during assembly")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
62000 neutrons/s, 21 during assembly
```
:::
:::


With illustrative values (a 6.2 kg core, 1% plutonium-240 emitting about
1000 neutrons per gram per second, 10 cm closed at 300 m/s), about
21 neutrons appear during assembly.
Predetonation is close to certain. Segrè's measurements of reactor
plutonium in 1944 showed this, and Los Alamos dropped the plutonium gun
[@hoddeson1993].

## Implosion

Implosion assembles the core in microseconds by crushing it. Compression
also lowers the critical mass. Both mean free paths scale as $1/\rho$, so
$R_c \propto 1/\rho$ and
$$
M_c = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi R_c^3 \rho \propto \frac{1}{\rho^2}.
$$
Doubling the density cuts the critical mass by four. The film credits Seth
Neddermeyer with the idea. Making it work needed explosive lenses to shape
a converging spherical shock, the problem George Kistiakowsky's division
solved; @hoddeson1993 is the detailed account.

# Trinity {#sec-trinity}

## The delay

The film's sound arrives well after the flash, which several reviewers
checked [@pitts2023; @griffith2023]. Sound in air travels at about
343 m/s:

::: {#93da6be9 .cell execution_count=13}
``` {.python .cell-code}
for miles in (6, 10):
    print(f"{miles} miles: {miles * 1609.34 / 343:.0f} s")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
6 miles: 28 s
10 miles: 47 s
```
:::
:::


## Fermi's paper strips

Fermi dropped scraps of paper as the blast wave passed base camp, about
16 km away, measured how far it moved them, and estimated the yield on the
spot. His memorandum records a displacement of about 2.5 m and an estimate
of about ten kilotons [@fermi1945].

## Taylor's dimensional analysis

In 1950 G. I. Taylor published the theory of a point explosion in air
[@taylor1950a] and applied it to photographs of the Trinity fireball that
had been released in 1947 [@taylor1950b]. If a large energy $E$ is
released at a point in gas of density $\rho_0$, at early times the shock
radius can depend only on $E$, $\rho_0$ and $t$. The only combination with
the dimension of length is
$$
R(t) = S(\gamma)\left(\frac{E\,t^2}{\rho_0}\right)^{1/5},
$$
where Taylor found $S \approx 1.03$ for air with $\gamma = 1.4$. Plotting
$\log R$ against $\log t$ should give a line of slope $2/5$, and its
intercept gives $E$.

::: {#cell-fig-taylor .cell execution_count=14}
``` {.python .cell-code}
trinity = np.array([  # t (ms), R (m), from Taylor (1950b)
    [0.10, 11.1], [0.24, 19.9], [0.38, 25.4], [0.52, 28.8], [0.66, 31.9],
    [0.80, 34.2], [0.94, 36.3], [1.08, 38.9], [1.22, 41.0], [1.36, 42.8],
    [1.50, 44.4], [1.65, 46.0], [1.79, 46.9], [1.93, 48.7], [3.26, 59.0],
    [3.53, 61.1], [3.80, 62.9], [4.07, 64.3], [4.34, 65.6], [4.61, 67.3],
    [15.0, 106.5], [25.0, 130.0], [34.0, 145.0], [53.0, 175.0],
    [62.0, 185.0]])
t_s, R_m = trinity[:, 0] / 1e3, trinity[:, 1]
slope, _ = np.polyfit(np.log(t_s), np.log(R_m), 1)
log_c = np.mean(np.log(R_m) - 0.4 * np.log(t_s))   # fix the slope at 2/5
rho_air, S_gamma = 1.25, 1.033
E_taylor = rho_air * np.exp(5 * log_c) / S_gamma**5

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3.2))
ax.loglog(t_s * 1e3, R_m, "o", ms=4, label="Taylor's data")
tt = np.logspace(-4.1, -1.1, 50)
ax.loglog(tt * 1e3, np.exp(log_c) * tt**0.4, label="slope 2/5")
ax.set_xlabel("t (ms)")
ax.set_ylabel("R (m)")
ax.legend()
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Radius of the Trinity shock front against time, from the photographs in Taylor (1950b), with the fitted line of slope 2/5.](index_files/figure-html/fig-taylor-output-1.png){#fig-taylor width=449 height=300}
:::
:::


The free fit has slope 0\.406, close to 0.4. With the
slope fixed at 2/5, $\rho_0 = 1.25$ kg/m³ and $S = 1.033$, the energy is
68 TJ, about 16
kilotons. Taylor's own figure was close to this. The yield was still
secret when he published, and the official figure today is about 21
kilotons. Rabi's guess of 18 kilotons, which won the film's betting pool,
was closer than either estimate.

@landau1987fluid [§106] derive the full self-similar solution, which gives $S(\gamma)$. They credit it to Sedov (1946) and von Neumann (1947), and note that Taylor's treatment, written in 1941 and published in 1950, stopped short of an analytic solution.

# The Super

The last act turns on the hydrogen bomb. The reaction that matters is
deuterium–tritium fusion:
$$
{}^2\mathrm H + {}^3\mathrm H \to {}^4\mathrm{He} + n.
$$

::: {#480606da .cell execution_count=15}
``` {.python .cell-code}
Q_DT = (mass["H2"] + mass["H3"] - mass["He4"] - mass["n"]) * u_MeV
print(f"Q = {Q_DT:.1f} MeV")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
Q = 17.6 MeV
```
:::
:::


It releases 17\.6 MeV, and the Coulomb barrier between
two charges of one is low enough for it to run at temperatures a fission
bomb can reach. Teller's wartime design, the "classical Super", tried to
start a burning wave in a cylinder of deuterium with a fission trigger.
Calculations in 1950 showed the wave would die out. The Teller–Ulam idea
of 1951 used radiation from the fission stage to compress the fusion fuel
first, the same lesson as implosion at a different scale. This is where
the open literature stops: the reports remain partly classified, and the
film keeps this part of the story to politics. The General Advisory
Committee report of October 1949, which Oppenheimer
chaired and which opposed a crash programme, is the document behind the
security hearing scenes; @bird2005 and @wellerstein2021 cover it.

*Textbooks:* @krane1988 [§14.5].

# Reading list

For the film itself, @griffith2023 and @whitfield2024. For the life,
@bird2005, which the film adapts. For the history of the project,
@rhodes1986. For the physics of the bomb, @reed2021, with @serber1992 as
the primary source and @hoddeson1993 for what Los Alamos actually did. For
secrecy and what it did to the literature, @wellerstein2021. For the
astrophysics, @oppenheimer1939snyder is five pages and readable today,
@ortega2017 explains its neglect, and @landau1975fields [§§102–103] and
@landau1980stat [§109] give the textbook treatment.

Most sections end with textbook references. Landau and Lifshitz are the
classic treatment. David Tong's Cambridge lecture notes are free online, so
every reader can follow those. @shankar1994 and @carroll2004 are the
standard modern texts for quantum mechanics and general relativity, and
@krane1988 for the nuclear physics.
